1.goal: To open on a meeting she really has at work, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine for a word she does not have.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class, and whether she wrote the note about a meeting.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she reads a short update and explains it to the CEO before a meeting.
Ask the question on screen and listen. Write down who is in the meeting and what she explains there.
exact: What today is: “Today you read an email about a problem at work. Then you explain it to the CEO before a meeting.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of one meeting. Who was there last time?”
1.expected: One real meeting, described in a few words or short sentences: who is there and what she usually explains or answers. A complete answer at this level looks like “Every Monday, meeting with the CEO and the other directors. I explain the projects of my area.” Portuguese words for the job or the company are acceptable here.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, offer two kinds of meeting and let her choose: a meeting with her team, or a call with people from another company.
1.challenge: Ask what is hardest for her in that meeting in English: understanding the questions, explaining, or asking.
1.monitoring: How long she takes to start, and whether she can describe the meeting in English with a few words.
1.evidence: The meeting she describes, in her words: participants, how often English is used, and what she has to do there.
1.transition: Move on when she has described one meeting.

2.goal: To establish who Paula is, what she needs, and what the explanation has to achieve.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the situation and the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “She needs to know the problem and what she has to decide.” The last line of the brief gives it: “Paula knows the problem and what she has to decide.” The problem itself is not on this screen; the email on screen 4 is where it appears.
2.support: If she starts guessing the problem, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what Paula would ask first, if the explanation were not clear.
2.monitoring: Whether she states the task from the brief, or starts talking about the content.
2.evidence: Whether she can say what Paula needs in one sentence without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she has said what Paula needs.

3.goal: To have her make three guesses from the subject line, so the first reading has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. The guesses stay open until the next screen.
run: Read the subject line and the three questions with her.
Take one answer for each question. Leave them unconfirmed: the email on the next screen settles them.
Write her three guesses where she can see them.
exact: If she does not risk a guess: “What could go wrong with new laptops?”
Before moving on: “These are your guesses. Now we read and check.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen. For your reference, the email shows that the laptops are late, that the sales team has a problem because their training comes first, and that Ryan needs a decision.
3.support: If she has no idea, offer two possibilities for the first question: the laptops are late, or the laptops do not work.
3.challenge: Ask which of her three guesses she is most sure about.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess or waits to read.
3.evidence: Her three guesses, kept for screen 4.
3.transition: Move on when the three questions have an answer.

4.goal: To read the email once for the main point: the problem and what Ryan needs.
run: Give her about two minutes to read the email once.
Ask the question on screen.
Then go back to her guesses from screen 3 and ask which ones the email confirms.
exact: Before she reads: “Read it once. Find two things: the problem, and what Ryan needs.”
4.expected: The problem: the new laptops did not arrive, and the sales team has training next Tuesday, before the new delivery date. What Ryan needs: a decision by Monday about the two options. A complete answer at this level: “The laptops are late, and the training is on Tuesday. Ryan needs a decision.”
4.support: If a word stops her, tell her to keep reading and come back to it at the end. Most of the words she might ask about were in the pre-class.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two options she would choose, before she reads the details.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads the whole email first or stops on words.
4.evidence: How long she took, whether she needed to reread, and which words she asked about.
4.transition: Move on when she has named the problem and what Ryan needs.

5.goal: To find the three true sentences, going back to the line in the email instead of answering from memory.
5.interaction: S says her answers and you mark them on screen, then T–S to check.
run: Read the six sentences with her. For each one, she says true or false and you mark her choice on screen. When three are marked, press Check. The button checks the whole activity at once.
Then go through the six out loud. On each one, open the email with the button on screen and ask her to read the line that decides it.
Spend the time that is left on the two false sentences that are easy to believe: the training is canceled, and the supplier needs an answer.
exact: On each sentence: “Which line says that? Read it to me.”
On the supplier sentence: “Who needs the decision: the supplier or Ryan?”
5.expected: True: “The laptops were supposed to arrive last Friday.” (“did not arrive last Friday”) · “The supplier had a problem at the warehouse.” (“The supplier had a problem at their warehouse”) · “The training is before the new delivery date.” (training next Tuesday, delivery next Thursday). False: “The training is canceled.” — moving it is only one option · “Ryan already chose one of the options.” — he needs a decision by Monday · “The supplier needs an answer by Monday.” — Ryan needs it, so he can tell the supplier and the trainer.
5.support: If she answers from memory, open the email and ask her to find the line before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask what Paula would lose if she thought the training was canceled.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the email, and which false sentence she marks.
5.evidence: Which false sentences she marked as true, and whether she found the lines without your help.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked and the two easy-to-believe sentences have been discussed.

6.goal: To have her notice that the lines of the email do four different jobs, before the jobs are explained.
6.interaction: S says her answers and you mark them on screen, then T–S to check.
run: For each of the six lines, she says the job and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each one, ask how she knew.
Leave the openings for the next screen: here she only sorts.
6.expected: What happened: “The new laptops for the sales team did not arrive last Friday.” · “The supplier had a problem at their warehouse, and the delivery is now next Thursday.” Why it is a problem: “The sales team has training on the new system next Tuesday.” · “Without the laptops, they cannot practice with the system in the training.” The options: “We move the training to the following week, or the sales team uses their old laptops.” What he needs: “I need a decision by Monday, so I can tell the supplier and the trainer.” The training line is the one most often placed in what happened: on its own it is a date, and next to the delivery date it is the problem.
6.support: On each line, ask: is this something that happened, or something Paula has to think about?
6.challenge: Ask her which part Paula needs most if she has only ten seconds.
6.monitoring: Whether she sees the job of the line, or only its topic.
6.evidence: Which lines she placed in a different job, and her reasons.
6.transition: Move on when the six lines are sorted.

7.goal: To have her notice the words that open a part, and to show the four openings after her answer.
run: Read the three lines on screen with her. The first words are in bold.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer before you open the button.
Open An update in four parts and read the four openings with her. Then ask her for one example of her own with two of the openings.
exact: If she talks about the content: “Forget the laptops. What do the bold words tell Paula?”
Asking for examples: “Give me a sentence about your work that starts with This is a problem because.”
7.expected: The bold words tell Paula what kind of information comes next: a reason why it matters, a choice, or a request. From the reveal, the four openings and their jobs: “A quick update: …” — what happened; “This is a problem because …” — why it matters; “We have two options: … or …” — the options; “I need a decision by …” — what you need, and when.
7.support: If she cannot say how a line goes on, give her two endings to choose from, or let her make her own: “This is a problem because… the client is waiting / the team cannot start the work.” · “We have two options:… we wait until Thursday, or we use the old ones / we call the supplier, or we change the date.” · “I need a decision by… Monday / the end of the day.”
7.challenge: Ask for another way to open the last part, for example “Could you let me know by …?”.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the idea before the reveal, and whether her examples use the openings correctly.
7.evidence: Her own examples, in her words.
7.transition: Move on when the openings have been read and she has given two examples.

8.goal: To hear situation A in four parts, and then to say situation B in four parts, starting each part with an opening, before the explanation to Paula.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one part at a time.
run: Read the notes for situation A with her. Then play situation A one part at a time. The words of each part stay hidden.
After each part, ask her to say the opening she heard, and then the whole part if she can.
Open the words of a part only if she needs to see them after two listens, and close them before the next part.
Then ask her to read the notes for situation B silently and to explain it in four parts, one at a time. When a part starts without an opening, ask her to say it again with the opening.
If there is time, she says situation A again in her own words, without the audio.
exact: Before situation A: “Listen to the first part. What does it start with?”
Starting situation B: “Tell me about the visitor badges. Start with: A quick update.”
Rebuilding a part: “Say that again, and start with: This is a problem because.”
8.expected: Situation A, the four parts she hears: “A quick update: the big room is not free on Friday.” — what happened · “This is a problem because the team meeting has twelve people.” — why it matters · “We have two options: we use two small rooms, or we have the meeting online.” — the options · “I need a decision by tomorrow.” — what you need. Situation B, one sentence per part: “A quick update: the visitor badges have the wrong names.” · “This is a problem because the visitors arrive on Monday.” · “We have two options: we print them again, or we use paper badges for one day.” · “I need an answer by Friday morning.” Other sentences that keep the four parts are correct.
8.support: If she cannot build a sentence for situation B from the notes, say the opening and the first word, and let her finish. If she does not catch a part of situation A after two listens, open the words for that part.
8.challenge: Ask her to add which option she prefers for situation B, with because.
8.monitoring: Whether she catches the opening of each part she hears, whether the openings stay when she builds the sentence from notes, and which words are hard to pronounce.
8.evidence: How many of the four parts of situation B started with an opening without help, and which parts of situation A needed the words on screen.
8.transition: Move on when she has said situation B in four parts.

9.goal: To explain the situation to Paula in four parts, with the sentence starters closed.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are Paula; she explains.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose.
Give her about a minute to make notes: single words, not sentences. With option B, ask her to say in one sentence what the situation is before she makes notes.
Let her explain. After two parts, interrupt once with the question below, and let her go back to where she was.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them if she stops, let her look, and close them again.
Leave corrections for screen 11. Write down one sentence as she said it.
exact: Opening: “Hi. I didn't read Ryan's email. What's the situation?”
The interruption, option A: “Sorry, when is the training?”
The interruption, option B: “Sorry, when did this happen?”
9.expected: Option A, four parts in one turn: what happened (the laptops did not arrive; the supplier had a warehouse problem; the delivery is now next Thursday); why it is a problem (the training is next Tuesday, and they cannot practice without the laptops); the options (move the training to the following week, or use the old laptops); what is needed (a decision by Monday). The answer to the interruption is “next Tuesday”. Option B has no fixed content: a complete explanation has the same four parts about her situation. Three to five sentences is a good result at this point; the profile describes answers with some support.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask which option she would choose, and why.
9.monitoring: Which parts appear, which openings she uses, and whether she returns to the explanation after the interruption.
9.evidence: The number of sentences in her turn, the parts she gave, and one sentence written word for word for screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has given the four parts, or has stopped after trying.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the explanation: answer two questions from Paula, say when she needs to check, and ask one question back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still Paula.
run: Ask the two questions below for the option she chose, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to finish or to say she can check.
Then ask her to put one question to you about the decision, and answer it.
exact: Option A, question 1: “Can the old laptops run the new system?”
Option A, question 2: “Which option do you prefer, and why?”
Option B, question 1: “Who else knows about this?”
Option B, question 2: “What happens if we do nothing?”
Handing the turn over: “Do you need anything else from me?”
10.expected: Option A: the email does not say whether the old laptops can run the new system, so a complete answer says she is not sure and can check, for example “I'm not sure. I can check with Ryan.” For the second question any option is acceptable with a reason: “I think we move the training, because they need the new laptops.” Option B: answers about her own situation, with the second one saying the consequence. Her question can be short, for example “When can you decide?” or “Do you want me to tell the sales director?”.
10.support: If she guesses an answer to the first question, ask “Does the email say that?” and wait.
10.challenge: Push back once: “I don't want to move the training. What else can we do?” Let her answer with an option.
10.monitoring: Whether she says she can check instead of inventing, and whether the question back comes without prompting.
10.evidence: Whether she said she could check, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the explanation again for a worried listener.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the sentence you noted on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. You are now the sales director, and you are worried about the training. She explains again in four parts and answers your worry.
exact: Opening the replay: “I heard there's a problem with the laptops. My team has the training on Tuesday. What's going on?”
11.expected: The same four parts, told to someone who is worried, with one sentence that answers the worry. A complete second version sounds like “I understand. The good news is we have two options: we move the training to the following week, or your team uses the old laptops.” — the worry acknowledged, and the options kept.
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: After her explanation, ask “So what should I tell my team today?” and let her answer.
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve changed in the second version.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you explain something at work, try to start with: A quick update.”
12.expected: The recap has six lines: reading a short update, finding what the email says and does not say, the four parts, the openings, explaining to the CEO, and answering questions or saying she needs to check. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one sentence she said today with an opening.
12.challenge: Ask which meeting this week she could use one opening in.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and the meeting she names for next week.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is the management meeting where Ryan talks about the laptops.
